mercy_translation.text:
Indeed, now that the common Savior of all has died on our behalf, we who believe in Christ no longer die as formerly under the threat of the law, for that condemnation has ceased. Rather, as corruption is brought to an end and disappears through the grace of the resurrection, we are dissolved only according to the mortality of the body, at the time God has appointed for each of us, so that we may obtain a better resurrection.

For like seeds cast into the earth, we are not destroyed when we are dissolved; rather, as though sown, we shall rise again, death having been abolished by the grace of the Savior. Therefore the blessed Paul, becoming a guarantor of the resurrection to all, says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. And when this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting?”

Why then, someone may ask, if it was necessary for him to hand over the body to death in place of all, did he not lay it aside privately as a human being, but proceed even to crucifixion? For it would seem more fitting that he lay down the body honorably than endure such a death with dishonor.

Consider again whether such an objection is not merely human, while what the Savior did was truly divine and worthy of his divinity for many reasons. First, the death that comes upon human beings comes to them because of the weakness of their nature. Since they cannot remain for a long time, they are dissolved by time. Thus diseases happen to them, and when they grow weak they die. But the Lord is not weak; he is the Power of God, the Word of God, and Life itself.

If, then, he had laid aside the body privately somewhere, in the ordinary way of human beings, upon a bed, it would have been supposed that he too suffered this because of the weakness of nature and possessed nothing more than other human beings. But because he was Life and the Word of God, and because a death on behalf of all had to take place, as Life and Power he strengthened the body in himself.

Yet because death had to occur, he did not take from himself the occasion for completing the sacrifice, but received it from others. For it was not fitting that the Lord, who healed the diseases of others, should himself become sick; nor was it fitting that the body by which he strengthened the weaknesses of others should itself become weak.

Why, then, did he not prevent death just as he prevented sickness? Because it was for death that he had the body, and it would have been unfitting to prevent it, lest the resurrection also be prevented. Yet it was again unfitting that sickness should precede his death, lest weakness be attributed to the One in the body. Did he not hunger? Yes, he hungered because this belonged to the body; but he did not perish from hunger because of the Lord who bore it. Therefore, although he died because of the ransom on behalf of all, “he did not see corruption.” He rose whole, because the body belonged not to another but to Life itself.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The seed analogy expresses Christian death as sowing toward resurrection rather than final destruction.
Athanasius distinguishes ordinary death from Christ's voluntary, representative death without denying the reality of Christ's bodily experiences.
